steps.headline: "Rules" is now "Advanced settings": closed cards whose titles say what the job does now.
steps.changed: Your C-rules note: each setting is a fold-out card, all closed when the popup opens. Open one and it says in one line what it covers, then lists its choices, each with one pro (+) and one con (−). "Wait up to" sits inside the first card.
steps.notice: A closed card's title changes with the choice ("Skips steps that need your OK", "Runs a missed run at 18:00"), so the list reads without opening anything.

steps.path: Where the permission list comes from
steps.headline: You don't build the list from a menu: the assistant writes it, and you check it.
steps.changed: Most automations start in a chat: "every Sunday, turn my new voice memos into notes". The assistant knows which folders, websites and commands it will use, so it writes each one as an exact permission ("See the files in ~/Recordings", "Run whisper on those files", "Change this page's information"). The check popup lists them in plain words before Turn on. Nothing on the list is a fixed catalogue, so a task nobody planned for works the same way.
steps.notice: The Add a permission menu is only for adding one yourself later; the next questions cover how that and the in-between cases work.

steps.headline: Offer "Try it once" before an automation is turned on?
steps.today: The check popup shows the drafted permissions and Turn on. The first real run is the first time anything is tested.
steps.problem: A drafted list can miss something (a second website, a folder the task needs), and you'd only find out when a scheduled run hits it.
steps.proposal: A practice run with you watching: anything not on the list asks you, and each Allow can add it to the list. When it finishes, you turn it on.

options.label: Offer Try it once
pros: Gaps show up while you're there, not at 3am.
cons: A practice run costs one run's usage or money.
One more button in the check popup.

options.label: No practice run
cons: Missed permissions surface only during real runs.

steps.path: A run asks about something not on its list
steps.headline: When a run asks about something not listed, offer "Allow from now on" too?
steps.today: The ask has Allow and Don't allow (with a note). Allow covers this one time only.
steps.problem: A task that needs it every week would ask every week, and the only other fix is adding the permission by hand.
steps.proposal: Three answers: Allow once, Allow from now on (adds that exact permission to the job's list), Don't allow (with a note).

options.label: Add Allow from now on
pros: The list grows from what the job really does.

options.label: Keep two buttons
cons: The same thing asks every run until you add it by hand.

steps.headline: Add "Describe it…" to the Add a permission menu?
steps.today: The menu lists a few kinds: a folder, a website, one command, this page's information.
steps.problem: Plenty of real needs fit none of these ("run my backup script", "use the printer"), and a fixed list can never cover them.
steps.proposal: Keep the few common kinds and add "Describe it…": you type it in your words, the assistant turns it into one exact permission and shows it back plainly before it's saved.

options.label: Common kinds + Describe it
pros: Quick for common cases, works for anything else.
cons: Describing needs a model, so it uses a little usage.

options.label: Common kinds only
cons: Anything else needs a chat with the assistant.

steps.path: A command that changes every run
steps.headline: How should a permission handle a command whose details change every run?
steps.today: "Run one command" allows that exact command only.
steps.problem: Most real commands change each time: "whisper memo-0412.m4a" this week, "whisper memo-0419.m4a" next week. An exact match would ask every run.
steps.proposal: Pick how wide a command permission is.

options.label: That program, any details
pros: Matches how Claude Code's own rules work.
cons: It could also point whisper at a file outside the listed folders.

steps.path: A permission to run your own script
steps.headline: If a script an automation may run is edited later, ask again before running it?
steps.today: "Run one script: ~/scripts/backup.sh" names the file, not what's in it.
steps.problem: If the file changes (you edit it, or another program does), the automation runs the new contents with the old permission.
steps.proposal: Remember the script as it was when you allowed it; if it changes, the next run asks first.

options.label: Ask again after a change
pros: A changed script never runs unseen.
cons: Your own edits cause one ask.

options.label: Trust the file name
cons: Whatever is in the file runs.

steps.path: What the assistant is told at the start of a run
steps.headline: Each run starts by telling the assistant its exact list and what happens to anything not on it.
steps.changed: Your Q-unlisted note ("make sure whatever the user selects is accurately conveyed to the model"): the run's opening instructions list each permission and its mode, then say in plain words: with Never, "don't try anything not listed; it will be refused"; with Asks first, "you may try it; the run waits for the person to answer". Tools it may never use are removed outright.
steps.notice: So with Asks first it does ask instead of quietly skipping, and with Never it doesn't keep trying.

steps.prompt: Anything still unclear, or to change
steps.headline: Anything about how permissions get built still unclear?
steps.today: This deck covers where the list comes from and how it grows.
